title: Multi-Task Learning as Multi-Objective Optimization
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2018)
problem_statement: Multi-task learning (MTL) is inherently a multi-objective optimization problem because tasks often compete and conflict for model capacity. Existing MTL methods commonly minimize a weighted linear combination of per-task losses, which requires expensive grid searches or heuristics and is only theoretically valid when tasks do not compete, failing to model task trade-offs and achieve Pareto optimality in high-dimensional deep networks.
domain: Multi-Task Deep Learning and Multi-Objective Optimization (Computer Vision)
theoretical_framework: Gradient-based multi-objective optimization and Pareto optimality via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, leveraging the Multiple-Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA) and Frank-Wolfe optimization, along with an upper-bound formulation (MGDA-UB) proving that optimizing representations yields Pareto stationary solutions when the representation Jacobian is full-rank.
methodology: The authors formulate multi-task learning as multi-objective optimization to find Pareto optimal solutions. They adapt the Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA) using a Frank-Wolfe optimizer with an exact analytical line search to solve the quadratic min-norm optimization in the convex hull of task gradients. To avoid scaling linearly with task count and gradient dimensions, they propose MGDA-UB (Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm – Upper Bound) for encoder-decoder architectures, which bounds the shared parameter objective by the norm of representation gradients using the chain rule. MGDA-UB optimizes representation gradients via a single backward pass over shared parameters, provably converging to a Pareto stationary point or a common descent direction assuming the Jacobian of the shared representation is full-rank.
datasets: MultiMNIST (MTL adaptation of MNIST with 60,000 overlaid digit image pairs for top-left and bottom-right classification tasks)
CelebA (CelebFaces Attributes dataset with 200,000 face images annotated with 40 binary attribute classification tasks)
Cityscapes (urban scene understanding dataset with pixel-level annotations for 19-class semantic segmentation, instance segmentation via center voting, and monocular depth estimation/disparity)
ImageNet (used for pretraining the ResNet-50 shared encoder backbone for Cityscapes)

metrics: Classification accuracy (%) on top-left digit (task-L) and bottom-right digit (task-R) for MultiMNIST
Mean classification error (%) and attribute-wise binary classification error (%) across 40 facial attributes for CelebA
Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) for semantic segmentation on Cityscapes
Mean Squared Error (MSE) of normalized pixel-level center offset regression for instance segmentation on Cityscapes
Mean Squared Error (MSE) of disparity estimation for depth estimation on Cityscapes
Wall-clock training time (seconds/hours) and GPU computational acceleration factor
baselines: Uniform scaling (minimizing a uniformly weighted sum of loss functions)
Single-task networks (solving each task independently with dedicated models)
Grid search (exhaustive evaluation of static loss weight combinations)
Uncertainty weighting (homoscedastic task uncertainty weighting by Kendall et al., 2018)
GradNorm (gradient normalization algorithm by Chen et al., 2018)
MGDA without approximation (full-parameter multiple gradient descent algorithm)
architectures: LeNet-based encoder with two task-specific fully-connected classification heads (MultiMNIST)
ResNet-18 shared backbone (without final layer) with 40 task-specific 2048x2 linear heads (CelebA)
Fully-convolutional ResNet-50 shared encoder with three task-specific Pyramid Pooling Module (PPM) decoders (Cityscapes)

key_findings: Formulating multi-task learning as multi-objective optimization with MGDA enables deep networks to find Pareto optimal solutions that effectively manage task trade-offs when tasks compete for model capacity.

On MultiMNIST, where competing tasks cause static scaling and heuristic weighting (Uncertainty Weighting, GradNorm) to underperform, MGDA-UB achieves digit classification accuracies comparable to dedicated single-task models (96.2% on task-L and 95.3% on task-R).

On the 40-task CelebA benchmark, MGDA-UB outperforms uniform scaling, single-task learning, uncertainty weighting, and GradNorm across the vast majority of attribute classification tasks, achieving the lowest average category error (8.95%).

On Cityscapes scene understanding, joint multi-task learning with MGDA-UB surpasses single-task and heuristic baselines across semantic segmentation (66.60 mIoU), instance segmentation (0.0104 MSE), and disparity estimation (0.0146 MSE).

MGDA-UB eliminates the computational bottleneck of standard MGDA by computing gradients with respect to shared representations via a single backward pass, accelerating training by 40% on Cityscapes (3 tasks) and by a factor of 25 on CelebA (40 tasks).

MGDA-UB achieves equal or slightly superior empirical accuracy compared to full-parameter MGDA because computing gradients in a lower-dimensional representation space reduces SGD gradient estimation variance and improves optimization stability.
scope_and_delimitations: Restricts theoretical guarantees and computational acceleration of MGDA-UB specifically to encoder-decoder and shared-trunk deep neural network architectures where task losses depend on a shared intermediate representation.
Assumes the Jacobian matrix of the shared representation with respect to shared parameters (dZ/d_theta_sh) is full rank to guarantee equivalence to Pareto stationarity.
Focuses on hard parameter sharing setups with gradient-based multi-objective optimization rather than soft parameter sharing or Bayesian prior regularization.
Evaluates on computer vision tasks (digit classification, facial attribute prediction, and dense scene understanding) with task counts ranging from 2 to 40.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: However, there are two technical problems that hinder the applicability of MGDA on a large scale. (i) The underlying optimization problem does not scale gracefully to high-dimensional gradients, which arise naturally in deep networks. (ii) The algorithm requires explicit computation of gradients per task, which results in linear scaling of the number of backward passes and roughly multiplies the training time by the number of tasks.
limitations.summary: Standard gradient-based multi-objective optimization (MGDA) scales poorly with gradient dimensionality and scales linearly with the number of tasks due to requiring separate backward passes for each task. Although the MGDA-UB approximation mitigates this, it relies on an encoder-decoder structure and assumes the representation Jacobian matrix is full rank.

generalizability_gap: The proposed method was evaluated exclusively on computer vision benchmarks (MultiMNIST, CelebA, and Cityscapes); the authors did not evaluate the approach on natural language processing, speech recognition, reinforcement learning, cross-modal learning, or large-scale foundation models.
methodological_gap: The MGDA-UB formulation is restricted to shared representation (encoder-decoder) architectures and requires the representation Jacobian to be non-singular (full rank); additionally, the method optimizes for arbitrary Pareto stationary points rather than allowing practitioners to target specific trade-off preferences along the Pareto front.
future_work: Extending gradient-based multi-objective optimization and representation-level bounds to non-vision domains such as natural language processing, speech processing, and multi-agent reinforcement learning.
Developing multi-objective optimization algorithms for complex multi-task architectures beyond encoder-decoder structures, such as branched networks or soft parameter sharing.
Investigating methods to steer multi-objective optimization toward specific desired trade-off regions or target points along the Pareto front.
